title: Test Method, Edge Cases and Big-O
tagline: Before Thursday. How to read, plan, test and submit so hidden test cases don't catch you.

topics.title: Reading the problem
topics.summary: Most failed submissions are misread problems, not bad algorithms.
items: Read the statement twice and restate it in one sentence
Write the input and output types and the constraints (n up to?)
Work through the given example by hand before coding
Spot the operation: is it `a / r` or `a - r`, contiguous or any subset, indices or values?
Ask: what should happen on empty input? (if the statement is silent, follow the examples)

questions.q: Explain your plan in 2 sentences before writing any code
questions.a:
Template: "I'll [core idea] using [data structure], which makes it O(...). Edge cases I'll handle are [empty / duplicates / ...]."
Example (Two Sum): "I'll walk the array once, storing each value's index in a dict, and for each number check whether target minus it is already there. That's O(n) time and O(n) space; I'll make sure a number can't pair with itself."

questions.q: Given n up to 10^5, which complexities are acceptable?
questions.a:
O(n), O(n log n), and O(n sqrt n) at a push. O(n^2) is 10^10 operations, far too slow.
So think: one pass with a hash map, sorting, two pointers, sliding window, binary search, or a heap.

concepts.title: Constraints tell you the algorithm
concepts.body:
The limit on n is a hint about the intended complexity. Roughly 10^7 to 10^8 simple operations run in a second.
- n up to 20: O(2^n) is fine (try all subsets)
- n up to 500: O(n^3)
- n up to 5,000: O(n^2)
- n up to 10^5 or 10^6: O(n log n) or O(n). Sorting, hashing, two pointers, sliding window
- n up to 10^9 or more: O(log n) or O(1). Binary search or maths
If your idea is O(n^2) and n is 10^5, it will time out on the hidden tests even if the samples pass.

topics.title: Edge cases and hidden tests
topics.summary: Hidden tests are mostly edge cases. Write yours first.
items: Before coding, write 3 to 5 tiny inputs with expected outputs
Always try: empty, one element, all equal, duplicates, negatives, zero
Try sorted and reverse-sorted input
Check first and last index (off-by-one) and window boundaries
Check the largest input mentally for time and for integer size
After a failed hidden test, re-read the statement before changing code

questions.q: What edge cases would you test for 'find the second largest number'?
questions.a:
- Empty list and a single element (no answer)
- All values equal, e.g. [3, 3, 3] (no distinct second)
- Duplicates of the maximum, e.g. [5, 1, 5, 2] → 2
- Negative numbers, e.g. [-4, -9] → -9
- Already sorted / reverse sorted
- And ask: what should be returned when there is no answer?

questions.q: Your code passes samples but fails 4 hidden tests. What do you do, in order?
questions.a:
1. Re-read the statement and constraints. Most hidden failures are a misread rule or an output format detail.
2. Check edge cases: empty, one element, duplicates, negatives, zero, max values.
3. If it's 'Time limit exceeded', your complexity is too high: look for an O(n) or O(n log n) approach.
4. Check off-by-one errors and integer division.
5. Write a tiny brute force and compare outputs on small random inputs if time allows.

resources: LeetCode problem 'Discuss' tabs for edge cases

concepts.title: The edge case checklist in practice
concepts.body:
Problem: return the second largest distinct value in a list, or -1 if there is none.
Cases to write before coding:
- [] → -1 (empty)
- [7] → -1 (one item)
- [3, 3, 3] → -1 (all equal, no distinct second)
- [5, 1, 5, 2] → 2 (duplicates of the max)
- [-4, -9] → -9 (negatives)
```python
def second_largest(a):
    first = second = None
    for x in a:
        if first is None or x > first:
            first, second = x, first
        elif x != first and (second is None or x > second):
            second = x
    return -1 if second is None else second
```
Note: returning -1 is ambiguous if -1 can be a real answer. Mention that out loud; interviewers like it.

topics.title: Big-O you must know cold
topics.summary: Know the cost of every built-in operation you use.
items: list: index O(1), append O(1), pop() O(1), pop(0) and insert(0) O(n), `x in list` O(n)
dict and set: get, add, `in` O(1) on average
sort / sorted: O(n log n); string concatenation in a loop: O(n^2), use ''.join
heapq push/pop O(log n), heapify O(n); deque append/popleft O(1)
Slicing a[i:j] copies: O(j - i)
Recursion depth limit in Python is about 1000: use iteration for deep inputs
Sorting: merge sort and heap sort O(n log n) worst case; quick sort O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst
Sorting: bubble, insertion and selection sort O(n^2); insertion sort is O(n) on nearly sorted data
Searching: linear O(n); binary search O(log n) but needs sorted data

questions.q: Why is `if x in my_list` inside a loop a problem, and what is the fix?
questions.a:
`in` on a list scans every element: O(n). Inside a loop of n items that becomes O(n^2).
Fix: build a set once (`s = set(my_list)`, O(n)), then each `x in s` is O(1) on average, so the whole thing is O(n).

questions.q: What is the time and space complexity of your solution?
questions.a:
How to answer: count the loops and what's inside them, then the extra memory.
- One pass with a dict: O(n) time, O(n) space
- Sort then scan: O(n log n) time, O(1) to O(n) space (Python's sort uses O(n))
- Two nested loops: O(n^2)
- Binary search: O(log n)
Say both, and mention the input size makes it fine (or not).

questions.q: Which sorting algorithm has the best asymptotic runtime: bubble, insertion, selection or merge?
questions.a:
Merge sort: O(n log n) in all cases. Bubble, insertion and selection are O(n^2).
If the options are bubble, selection, heap and insertion, the answer is heap sort (also O(n log n)).

concepts.title: Sorting and searching cheat sheet (common multiple-choice)
concepts.body:
- Merge sort: O(n log n) best, average and worst. O(n) extra space. Stable.
- Heap sort: O(n log n) always. O(1) extra space. Not stable.
- Quick sort: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst (bad pivots). In place. Usually fastest in practice.
- Insertion sort: O(n^2) worst, O(n) best (already sorted). Good for small or nearly sorted data.
- Bubble sort and selection sort: O(n^2). Never the right answer for 'best'.
- Counting / radix sort: O(n + k), only for integers in a limited range.
- Python's sorted() and JS's Array.prototype.sort (V8) use Timsort: O(n log n) worst, O(n) on sorted input, stable.
- Linear search O(n); binary search O(log n) on sorted data; hash lookup O(1) average.
Typical question: 'best asymptotic runtime' among bubble / insertion / selection / merge → merge sort.

topics.title: Python tools for speed
topics.summary: The standard library does half the work.
items: collections.Counter, defaultdict(int), defaultdict(list), deque
zip(a, a[1:]) for neighbours; enumerate for index and value
sorted(x, key=lambda t: (t[1], -t[0])) for multi-key sorts
bisect_left / bisect_right for binary search in a sorted list
heapq (min-heap; push -x for a max-heap)
itertools: accumulate (prefix sums), combinations, permutations, product

questions.q: Write a one-liner that counts how many values appear exactly twice
questions.a:
```python
from collections import Counter
sum(1 for c in Counter(arr).values() if c == 2)
# or
Counter(Counter(arr).values())[2]
```

resources: Python docs: collections, heapq, bisect, itertools

concepts.title: Templates to type without thinking
concepts.body:
```python
from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque
from itertools import accumulate
import heapq, bisect

freq = Counter(arr)                       # value -> count
groups = defaultdict(list)                # key -> list
prefix = [0, *accumulate(arr)]            # sum(arr[i:j]) == prefix[j] - prefix[i]
pairs = list(zip(arr, arr[1:]))           # neighbours
i = bisect.bisect_left(sorted_arr, x)     # first index with value >= x
heap = []; heapq.heappush(heap, (dist, node)); d, n = heapq.heappop(heap)
q = deque([start]); q.append(x); q.popleft()
```

topics.title: DSA in JavaScript (backup language)
topics.summary: If the test only allows JS/TS, these are the same patterns.
items: Set for lookups: new Set(arr), s.has(x), s.add(x), s.size
Map for counting: m.set(x, (m.get(x) ?? 0) + 1); iterate with for (const [k, v] of m)
Numeric sort ALWAYS needs a comparator: arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)
Integer division Math.floor(a / b) (or Math.trunc for negatives); % keeps the sign (-1 % 3 === -1)
Arrays: push/pop O(1), shift/unshift O(n): use an index pointer as a queue
No built-in heap: sort once, or use a small binary heap, or the test's provided helper
Big integers: Number is safe up to 2^53 - 1; use BigInt (10n) beyond that
Use the HackerRank input template; don't write your own stdin parsing

questions.a:
JavaScript's default sort converts items to strings and compares them alphabetically. "1" < "10" (prefix) and "10" < "9" (first char '1' < '9').
Fix: `arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)` for ascending numbers (`b - a` for descending).

questions.q: How do you count frequencies in JS?
How do you implement a queue in JS without O(n) shift?

concepts.title: Python → JavaScript, side by side

Which complexity fits n = 10^5 and why
The cost of `in` on a list vs a set
mustDo: Do the HackerRank sample test end to end, timed
Solve one easy problem writing edge cases BEFORE the code

configs.title: Submission routine
configs.note: Do this every time, even in practice.
configs.code:
1. Read twice. Restate in one sentence.
2. Note constraints -> target complexity.
3. Write 3-5 edge cases with expected outputs.
4. Brute force idea first (say it), then optimise.
5. Code. Run the samples. Run your edge cases.
6. Re-read the statement. Submit.

title: Logic Puzzles and Maths for Coding
tagline: Before Thursday. The recruiter mentioned puzzles: pattern spotting, quick maths and number tricks.

topics.title: Logic and pattern puzzles
topics.summary: Slow down, write it out, check every option.
items: Number sequences: check differences, ratios, squares/cubes, alternating patterns, Fibonacci-like sums
Letter sequences: convert to positions (A=1 ... Z=26) and look at the gaps
Truth-teller / liar puzzles: assume one case, follow it until it contradicts
Ordering puzzles (who sits where): draw a grid and fill fixed facts first
Odd one out: find the rule most items share
Eliminate wrong multiple-choice options instead of solving from scratch

questions.a: 42. Differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next is +12. (It's also n x (n+1).)
13. Fibonacci: each number is the sum of the two before it.
243. Multiply by 3 each time (powers of 3).

questions.q: Next letters: A, C, F, J, O, ?
questions.a: U. Positions 1, 3, 6, 10, 15: gaps 2, 3, 4, 5, so the next gap is 6 → 21 = U.

concepts.title: Answers and the trick behind each
concepts.body:
- 2, 6, 12, 20, 30 → 42. Differences 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. (Also n x (n+1).)
- 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 → 13. Each is the sum of the previous two.
- 3, 9, 27, 81 → 243. Multiply by 3.
- A, C, F, J, O → U. Positions 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21: gaps grow by 1.
First thing to try on any sequence: write the differences underneath. If those don't help, try ratios, then squares.

topics.title: Classic brain teasers
topics.summary: The well-known ones come up again and again.
items: Weighing: find the heavier ball among 8 with 2 weighings (split into 3 groups, not 2)
Clock angle: |30h - 5.5m| degrees, take 360 minus it if over 180
Handshakes / pairs: n(n-1)/2
Rates: 'work together' problems add rates (1/a + 1/b)
Average speed for equal distances is the harmonic mean, not the plain average
Probability basics: independent events multiply; 'at least one' = 1 - P(none)

questions.a:
7.5 degrees. Formula |30h - 5.5m| = |90 - 82.5| = 7.5.
(The hour hand has moved a quarter of the way from 3 to 4 by 3:15, which is why it isn't 0.)

questions.q: 10 people each shake hands once with everyone. How many handshakes?
questions.a: 45. n(n-1)/2 = 10 x 9 / 2. Each pair shakes once.

questions.q: Tap A fills a tank in 3h, tap B in 6h. Together?
questions.a: 2 hours. Add rates: 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2 tank per hour.

questions.q: Go 60 km/h there and 40 km/h back. Average speed?
questions.a:
48 km/h, not 50. For equal distances use the harmonic mean: 2 x 60 x 40 / (60 + 40) = 48.
(You spend longer at the slower speed, so it pulls the average down.)

concepts.title: Answers
concepts.body:
- 3:15 → |30x3 - 5.5x15| = |90 - 82.5| = 7.5 degrees
- 10 people → 10 x 9 / 2 = 45 handshakes
- Taps → 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2 tank per hour → 2 hours
- 60 and 40 → 2 x 60 x 40 / (60 + 40) = 48 km/h (not 50)
- 8 balls, one heavier, 2 weighings: weigh 3 vs 3. If equal, weigh the last 2. If not, take the heavy 3 and weigh 1 vs 1.

topics.title: Maths that shows up in code
topics.summary: Small number facts that turn into coding questions.
items: Modulo: even/odd, wrap-around indexes (i + 1) % n, last digit x % 10
Digits: sum of digits with while n: n, d = divmod(n, 10)
GCD and LCM: math.gcd; lcm = a * b // gcd(a, b)
Primes: trial division up to sqrt(n); sieve for many numbers
Powers of two: n & (n - 1) == 0 (for n > 0); count bits with bin(n).count('1')
Sum 1..n = n(n+1)/2: find the missing number in O(1) space
Large results: answer modulo 10^9 + 7 when the statement asks

questions.a:
Sum formula: expected n(n+1)/2 minus the actual sum. O(n) time, O(1) space.
```python
def missing(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    return n * (n + 1) // 2 - sum(nums)
```
Alternative: XOR all indices and values; pairs cancel and the missing one remains.

questions.q: Is a number a power of two?
questions.a:
`n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0`. A power of two has exactly one 1-bit, and n - 1 flips it and all bits below it, so the AND is 0.
Don't forget n > 0 (0 and negatives are not powers of two).

questions.q: Check if a number is a palindrome without converting to a string
questions.a:
Reverse the digits arithmetically and compare.
```python
def is_pal(x):
    if x < 0: return False
    orig, rev = x, 0
    while x:
        x, d = divmod(x, 10)
        rev = rev * 10 + d
    return rev == orig
```
Edge cases: negatives (False), 0 (True), numbers ending in 0 like 10 (False).

questions.q: FizzBuzz (yes, really: get the edge cases right)

concepts.title: Templates
concepts.body:
```python
import math
def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2: return False
    for d in range(2, math.isqrt(n) + 1):
        if n % d == 0: return False
    return True

def missing(nums):                  # nums has 0..n with one missing
    n = len(nums)
    return n * (n + 1) // 2 - sum(nums)

def digit_sum(n):
    s = 0
    while n:
        n, d = divmod(n, 10); s += d
    return s

is_pow2 = lambda n: n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0
```
In JavaScript: Math.floor(a / b) for integer division, and watch out because % keeps the sign (-1 % 3 is -1).

mustKnow: Write differences first on any sequence
Clock angle, handshakes, combined rates and average speed formulas
Modulo, gcd, primes up to sqrt(n), the n(n+1)/2 trick
mustDo: Solve 10 sequence/logic questions under time (about 1 minute each)
Write is_prime, missing number and is_pow2 from memory

configs.title: Puzzle routine
configs.code:
1. Read the question once slowly. Underline what is asked.
2. Write it down: differences, a grid, or a quick sketch.
3. Check each option against the rule; eliminate.
4. Stuck after ~90 seconds? Pick the best guess, flag it, move on.
5. Come back to flagged ones at the end, if the test allows going back (check this in the sample test).

title: CS Fundamentals for Multiple Choice
tagline: Before Thursday. The theory questions the sample test hinted at, with answers.

topics.title: Data structures and their costs
topics.summary: Know what each structure is good and bad at.
items: Array: index O(1), insert/delete in the middle O(n), search O(n) (O(log n) if sorted)
Linked list: insert/delete at a known node O(1), index and search O(n)
Stack = LIFO (undo, brackets, call stack, DFS); Queue = FIFO (BFS, task scheduling)
Hash table: insert/lookup/delete O(1) average, O(n) worst (many collisions); no order
Collisions handled by chaining or open addressing; a good hash and resizing keep it O(1)
Heap: get min/max O(1), insert and remove O(log n); used for priority queues
Balanced BST: search/insert/delete O(log n); unbalanced worst case O(n)
Graph representations: adjacency list (sparse, O(V+E) space) vs matrix (dense, O(V^2))

questions.q: Which structure gives O(1) average lookup by key?
questions.a: A hash table (Python dict/set, JS Map/Set/object). Worst case O(n) with many collisions.

questions.q: Which structure is used for BFS? And for DFS?
questions.a: BFS uses a queue (FIFO, level by level). DFS uses a stack, either explicit or the call stack via recursion.

questions.q: Worst-case search in an unbalanced BST?
questions.a: O(n). Inserting sorted data makes the tree a straight line, like a linked list. Balanced trees (AVL, red-black) keep it O(log n).

questions.q: Best structure to always get the smallest item quickly?
questions.a: A min-heap: peek O(1), insert and remove-min O(log n). In Python, heapq.

concepts.title: Practice MCQs with answers
concepts.body:
1. Accessing the 5th element of an array is: O(1). In a linked list: O(n).
2. Undo in a text editor is best modelled with a: stack.
3. A printer job list is best modelled with a: queue.
4. Average time to check membership in a hash set: O(1). Worst case: O(n).
5. Height of a balanced binary tree with n nodes: O(log n).
6. Inserting into a binary heap: O(log n). Building a heap from n items: O(n).
7. Space of an adjacency matrix for V vertices: O(V^2).
8. Which is NOT O(n log n) in the worst case: merge sort, heap sort, quick sort? → quick sort (O(n^2)).

topics.title: Trees, traversals and recursion
topics.summary: Trace small examples by hand.
items: In-order (left, node, right) of a BST gives sorted order
Pre-order (node, left, right) and post-order (left, right, node)
Level-order = BFS with a queue
Recursion needs a base case; each call uses stack space (O(depth))
Naive recursive Fibonacci is O(2^n); with memoisation O(n)
Binary search tree: left < node < right

questions.q: In-order traversal of the BST built by inserting 5, 3, 8, 1, 4?
questions.a: 1 3 4 5 8. In-order of any BST gives sorted order.
5 3 1 4 8 (node, then left subtree, then right subtree).

questions.q: What does f(4) return if f(n) = n * f(n-1), f(0) = 1?
questions.a: 24. It's factorial: 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 x 1.

concepts.title: Trace it
concepts.body:
Insert 5, 3, 8, 1, 4 into an empty BST:
```text
      5
     / \
    3   8
   / \
  1   4
```
- In-order: 1 3 4 5 8 (sorted)
- Pre-order: 5 3 1 4 8
- Post-order: 1 4 3 8 5
- Level-order: 5 3 8 1 4
```python
def f(n):
    if n <= 1: return n
    return f(n - 1) + f(n - 2)
# f(5) = 5. Calls grow like 2^n, so f(40) is very slow without @cache.
```

topics.title: Binary, bits and number systems
topics.summary: Quick conversions and bit operators.
items: Convert decimal to binary by powers of 2: 13 = 8 + 4 + 1 = 1101
Hex: 0xFF = 255; one hex digit = 4 bits
AND (&), OR (|), XOR (^), NOT (~), shifts (<<, >>); x << 1 doubles, x >> 1 halves
x & 1 tells odd/even; x ^ x = 0 (find the single non-duplicate)
n bits can represent 2^n values; a byte is 8 bits (0 to 255 unsigned)

questions.q: How many values can 10 bits represent?

topics.title: OOP and 'what does this print?'
topics.summary: Read code carefully, line by line.
items: Encapsulation (hide internals), inheritance (reuse), polymorphism (same call, different behaviour), abstraction
Overriding (subclass replaces a method) vs overloading (same name, different parameters)
Composition over inheritance; interfaces / abstract classes
Pass by value vs reference: objects and lists are shared, reassignment is not
Trace loops by writing variable values in a small table
Integer division and modulo differ by language: Python 7 // 2 = 3, -7 // 2 = -4; JS Math.trunc(-7 / 2) = -3

questions.q: What does this print? x = [1, 2]; y = x; y.append(3); print(x)
questions.a: [1, 2, 3]. `y = x` copies the reference, not the list. Use `y = x.copy()` or `x[:]` for a shallow copy.

- Overriding: a subclass provides its own version of a method with the same signature (runtime polymorphism).
- Overloading: same method name, different parameter lists in the same class (compile-time; Java/C# have it, Python and JS don't natively).

- Encapsulation: hide internal state behind methods
- Abstraction: expose what something does, not how
- Inheritance: reuse behaviour from a parent class
- Polymorphism: the same call behaves differently for different types

concepts.body:

```python
total = 0
for i in range(1, 6):
    if i % 2 == 0:
        continue
    total += i
print(total)        # 9  (1 + 3 + 5)

def add(item, box=[]):     # default list is shared between calls!
    box.append(item)

add(1); print(add(2))      # [1, 2]
```
```js
let a = { n: 1 }; let b = a; b.n = 2;
console.log(a.n);          // 2 (same object)
let c = 1; let d = c; d = 5;
console.log(c);            // 1 (numbers are copied)
```

title: Arrays, Strings and Hash Maps
tagline: Before Thursday. The most common test pattern: count, look up, group.

topics.title: Counting and frequency
topics.summary: When the question is about how many times, reach for a Counter.
items: Count with Counter or defaultdict(int)
Count the counts: Counter(Counter(s).values())
Anagrams: compare Counters, or sorted strings as keys
First unique character: count first, then scan in order
Majority element and top-k frequent (Counter.most_common)

questions.a:
Same letters with the same counts. O(n).
```python
from collections import Counter
def is_anagram(s, t): return len(s) == len(t) and Counter(s) == Counter(t)
```

questions.q: First Unique Character in a String
questions.a:
Count first, then scan in order for count 1. O(n).
```python
from collections import Counter
def first_unique(s):
    c = Counter(s)
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        if c[ch] == 1: return i
    return -1
```

Count, then take the k most common. O(n log k) with a heap.
```python
from collections import Counter
def top_k(nums, k): return [x for x, _ in Counter(nums).most_common(k)]
```
O(n) alternative: bucket sort by frequency.

Valid if all letters appear equally often, or can be after removing one character.
```python
from collections import Counter
def is_valid(s):
    freq = Counter(Counter(s).values())      # count -> how many letters have it
    if len(freq) == 1: return "YES"
    if len(freq) > 2: return "NO"
    (a, na), (b, nb) = sorted(freq.items())  # a < b
    if a == 1 and na == 1: return "YES"      # one letter appears once: remove it
    if b == a + 1 and nb == 1: return "YES"  # one letter has one extra
    return "NO"
```

concepts.title: Group anagrams

topics.title: Look up a partner (seen-so-far)
topics.summary: One pass: for each item, ask whether its partner was already seen.
items: Two Sum with a dict value -> index, checked before inserting
Pairs with difference k using a set
Contains duplicate (within distance k): dict of last index
Count pairs/triplets by updating counts in the right order
Know when you need a set (exists?) vs a dict (count or index)

questions.a:
Geometric triplets (a, a*r, a*r*r) with i < j < k. Track singles and pairs ending at each value. O(n).
```python
from collections import defaultdict
def count_triplets(arr, r):
    singles, pairs, res = defaultdict(int), defaultdict(int), 0
    for a in arr:
        if a % r == 0:
            prev = a // r
            res += pairs[prev]          # a completes triplets
            pairs[a] += singles[prev]   # a extends pairs
        singles[a] += 1
    return res
```
Order matters: use counts from before adding a. Works for r = 1 too.

Put everything in a set; only start counting from numbers with no predecessor. O(n).
```python
def longest(nums):
    s, best = set(nums), 0
    for x in s:
        if x - 1 not in s:
            y = x
            while y + 1 in s: y += 1
            best = max(best, y - x + 1)
    return best
```

concepts.title: Two Sum, the pattern behind many problems
concepts.body:
```python
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                      # value -> index
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if target - x in seen:     # check BEFORE inserting, so x can't pair with itself
            return [seen[target - x], i]
        seen[x] = i
    return []
```

topics.title: Prefix sums
topics.summary: Precompute running totals to answer range sums in O(1).
items: Build prefix = [0, *accumulate(arr)]
Range sum arr[i..j] = prefix[j+1] - prefix[i]
Subarray sum equals k: dict of prefix-sum counts
Difference array for many range updates

questions.a:
Precompute prefix sums; each query is O(1).
```python
from itertools import accumulate
class NumArray:
    def __init__(self, nums): self.p = [0, *accumulate(nums)]
    def sumRange(self, i, j): return self.p[j + 1] - self.p[i]
```

Prefix sums + a dict counting how many times each prefix appeared. O(n). Works with negatives.
```python
from collections import defaultdict
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    seen = defaultdict(int); seen[0] = 1
    total = ans = 0
    for x in nums:
        total += x
        ans += seen[total - k]
        seen[total] += 1
    return ans
```

Add k to range [a, b] many times, then find the max. Mark +k at a and -k after b, then prefix-sum. O(n + m).
```python
def array_manipulation(n, queries):
    diff = [0] * (n + 2)
    for a, b, k in queries:
        diff[a] += k; diff[b + 1] -= k
    best = cur = 0
    for v in diff:
        cur += v; best = max(best, cur)
    return best
```

concepts.title: Subarray sum equals k
concepts.body:
A subarray ending at i sums to k when some earlier prefix equals current_prefix - k.
```python
from collections import defaultdict
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    count = defaultdict(int); count[0] = 1   # empty prefix
    total = ans = 0
    for x in nums:
        total += x
        ans += count[total - k]
        count[total] += 1
    return ans
```
Works with negatives (a sliding window does not). Forgetting count[0] = 1 is the classic bug.

questions.a:
Two pointers, skipping non-alphanumerics, comparing lowercase. O(n), O(1) space.
```python
def is_pal(s):
    i, j = 0, len(s) - 1
    while i < j:
        if not s[i].isalnum(): i += 1
        elif not s[j].isalnum(): j -= 1
        elif s[i].lower() != s[j].lower(): return False
        else: i += 1; j -= 1
    return True
```

"aaabcc" → "a3bc2" style: walk runs with two pointers.
```python
def compress(s):
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(s):
        j = i
        while j < len(s) and s[j] == s[i]: j += 1
        out.append(s[i] + (str(j - i) if j - i > 1 else ""))
        i = j
    return "".join(out)
```
(LeetCode's version modifies a char array in place, same idea.)

topics.title: Two pointers
topics.summary: Two indices moving toward each other or in the same direction.
items: Opposite ends on a sorted array (pair sum, container)
Fast/slow pointers to remove duplicates in place

Sort first when order does not matter, then two pointers

questions.a:
Sorted input: two pointers from both ends. O(n), O(1) space.
```python
def two_sum_sorted(a, t):
    i, j = 0, len(a) - 1
    while i < j:
        s = a[i] + a[j]
        if s == t: return [i + 1, j + 1]   # LeetCode wants 1-based
        if s < t: i += 1
        else: j -= 1
```

Start wide; always move the shorter wall inward (the taller can't help while the short one limits height). O(n).
```python
def max_area(h):
    i, j, best = 0, len(h) - 1, 0
    while i < j:
        best = max(best, (j - i) * min(h[i], h[j]))
        if h[i] < h[j]: i += 1
        else: j -= 1
    return best
```

Sort, fix one number, two-pointer the rest, skip duplicates. O(n^2).
```python
def three_sum(nums):
    nums.sort(); res = []
    for i in range(len(nums) - 2):
        if i and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]: continue
        l, r = i + 1, len(nums) - 1
        while l < r:
            s = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r]
            if s < 0: l += 1
            elif s > 0: r -= 1
            else:
                res.append([nums[i], nums[l], nums[r]])
                l += 1
                while l < r and nums[l] == nums[l - 1]: l += 1
    return res
```

Fill from the back so you don't overwrite nums1. O(m + n).
```python
def merge(n1, m, n2, n):
    i, j, k = m - 1, n - 1, m + n - 1
    while j >= 0:
        if i >= 0 and n1[i] > n2[j]: n1[k] = n1[i]; i -= 1
        else: n1[k] = n2[j]; j -= 1
        k -= 1
```

concepts.body:
```python
def pair_with_sum(sorted_arr, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(sorted_arr) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        s = sorted_arr[lo] + sorted_arr[hi]
        if s == target: return lo, hi
        if s < target: lo += 1     # need bigger
        else: hi -= 1              # need smaller
    return None
```

topics.title: Sliding window
topics.summary: Contiguous block: add the entering item, remove the leaving one.
items: Fixed size k: compute first window, then slide
Variable size: expand right, shrink left while invalid
Track window contents with a Counter or set
Spot it: 'contiguous', 'substring', 'subarray of length k', 'at most k'

questions.a:
Fixed window of size k: slide and keep the best sum, divide at the end. O(n).
```python
def max_avg(nums, k):
    cur = best = sum(nums[:k])
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        cur += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best / k
```

Variable window; jump left past the last occurrence of a repeat. O(n).
```python
def longest_unique(s):
    last, left, best = {}, 0, 0
    for r, ch in enumerate(s):
        if last.get(ch, -1) >= left: left = last[ch] + 1
        last[ch] = r
        best = max(best, r - left + 1)
    return best
```

Shortest window with sum >= target (positive numbers). Expand right, shrink left while valid. O(n).
```python
def min_len(target, nums):
    left = total = 0; best = float("inf")
    for r, x in enumerate(nums):
        total += x
        while total >= target:
            best = min(best, r - left + 1)
            total -= nums[left]; left += 1
    return 0 if best == float("inf") else best
```

Window is valid if (window length - count of most common char) <= k. O(n).
```python
from collections import defaultdict
def char_replace(s, k):
    count = defaultdict(int); left = top = best = 0
    for r, ch in enumerate(s):
        count[ch] += 1; top = max(top, count[ch])
        while (r - left + 1) - top > k:
            count[s[left]] -= 1; left += 1
        best = max(best, r - left + 1)
    return best
```
(top never needs decreasing; the answer only grows when top grows.)

Answer = sum of servers already on + best window of length k counting only servers that are off. O(n).
```python
def max_performance(perf, on, k):
    base = sum(p for p, s in zip(perf, on) if s)
    gain = sum(p for p, s in zip(perf[:k], on[:k]) if not s)
    best = gain
    for i in range(k, len(perf)):
        if not on[i]: gain += perf[i]
        if not on[i - k]: gain -= perf[i - k]
        best = max(best, gain)
    return base + best
```

concepts.title: Variable window template
concepts.body:
```python
def longest_unique(s):
    last = {}                 # char -> last index
    left = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last and last[ch] >= left:
            left = last[ch] + 1          # shrink past the repeat
        last[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
```
Edge cases: "", "a", "aaaa", all unique.

topics.title: Binary search
topics.summary: Halve the search space; also works on the answer itself.
items: Classic search in a sorted array with lo <= hi
First/last position (lower and upper bound)
Search on the answer: smallest x where condition(x) is true
Rotated sorted array
Use bisect when you just need positions

questions.a:
```python
def search(a, t):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] == t: return mid
        if a[mid] < t: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1
```
O(log n). Edge cases: empty array, target at either end, not present.
Lower bound: the first index with a[i] >= target. `bisect.bisect_left(a, target)` does exactly this, O(log n).

Two binary searches: first index >= t and first index > t.
```python
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
def search_range(a, t):
    l = bisect_left(a, t)
    if l == len(a) or a[l] != t: return [-1, -1]
    return [l, bisect_right(a, t) - 1]
```

Binary search on the answer: smallest speed s with total hours <= h. O(n log max).
```python
def min_speed(piles, h):
    lo, hi = 1, max(piles)
    while lo < hi:
        s = (lo + hi) // 2
        if sum((p + s - 1) // s for p in piles) <= h: hi = s
        else: lo = s + 1
    return lo
```
`(p + s - 1) // s` is ceiling division.

At each step one half is sorted; check if the target lies in that half. O(log n).
```python
def search(a, t):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        m = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[m] == t: return m
        if a[lo] <= a[m]:                     # left half sorted
            if a[lo] <= t < a[m]: hi = m - 1
            else: lo = m + 1
        else:                                 # right half sorted
            if a[m] < t <= a[hi]: lo = m + 1
            else: hi = m - 1
    return -1
```

concepts.title: Lower-bound template (no off-by-one)
concepts.body:
```python
def first_true(lo, hi, ok):      # smallest x in [lo, hi] with ok(x) True; hi if none
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if ok(mid): hi = mid
        else: lo = mid + 1
    return lo
```

questions.a:
Iterative: save next, point back, move forward. O(n), O(1) space.
```python
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    while head:
        nxt = head.next; head.next = prev; prev = head; head = nxt
    return prev
```

Dummy head + tail pointer; attach the smaller node each time, then the leftover.
```python
def merge(a, b):
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val: tail.next, a = a, a.next
        else: tail.next, b = b, b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b
    return dummy.next
```

Floyd's tortoise and hare: slow moves 1, fast moves 2; if they meet, there's a cycle. O(n), O(1) space.
```python
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
        if slow is fast: return True
    return False
```

questions.q: Remove Nth Node From End of List
questions.a:
Move `fast` n steps ahead, then move both until fast reaches the end; slow is just before the node to delete. Use a dummy head for removing the first node.
```python
def remove_nth(head, n):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head); slow = fast = dummy
    for _ in range(n): fast = fast.next
    while fast.next: slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next
    slow.next = slow.next.next
    return dummy.next
```

```python
        head.next, prev, head = prev, head, head.next

```

```python
    if not n: return True
    if not lo < n.val < hi: return False
```

questions.a:
Walk from the root: if both values are smaller go left, both bigger go right, otherwise this node splits them. O(h).
```python
def lca(root, p, q):
    while root:
        if p.val < root.val and q.val < root.val: root = root.left
        elif p.val > root.val and q.val > root.val: root = root.right
        else: return root
```

questions.a:
DFS from the start cell, recolouring cells that match the original colour. Return early if the new colour equals the old one (otherwise infinite loop).
```python
def flood_fill(img, r, c, new):
    old = img[r][c]
    if old == new: return img
    def fill(r, c):
        if 0 <= r < len(img) and 0 <= c < len(img[0]) and img[r][c] == old:
            img[r][c] = new
            fill(r+1, c); fill(r-1, c); fill(r, c+1); fill(r, c-1)
    fill(r, c)
    return img
```

Can you finish all courses? Equivalent to "is there no cycle?". Kahn's topological sort: repeatedly take courses with no remaining prerequisites.
```python
from collections import deque, defaultdict
def can_finish(n, prereqs):
    g, indeg = defaultdict(list), [0] * n
    for a, b in prereqs: g[b].append(a); indeg[a] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0); taken = 0
    while q:
        x = q.popleft(); taken += 1
        for y in g[x]:
            indeg[y] -= 1
            if indeg[y] == 0: q.append(y)
    return taken == n
```

DFS/BFS with a dict old node → new node, so each node is copied once and cycles don't loop forever.
```python
def clone(node, seen=None):
    if not node: return None
    seen = {} if seen is None else seen
    if node in seen: return seen[node]
    copy = Node(node.val); seen[node] = copy
    copy.neighbors = [clone(n, seen) for n in node.neighbors]
    return copy
```

concepts.title: Grid BFS template
concepts.body:
```python
from collections import deque
def bfs(grid, start):
    R, C = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    dist = {start: 0}; q = deque([start])
    while q:
        r, c = q.popleft()
        for dr, dc in ((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)):
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            if 0 <= nr < R and 0 <= nc < C and grid[nr][nc] != '#' and (nr, nc) not in dist:
                dist[(nr, nc)] = dist[(r, c)] + 1
                q.append((nr, nc))
    return dist
```

questions.q: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
questions.a:
Track the cheapest price so far; profit = today - cheapest. O(n).
```python
def max_profit(prices):
    low, best = float("inf"), 0
    for p in prices:
        low = min(low, p); best = max(best, p - low)

```

Track the furthest index reachable; if you ever stand beyond it, you're stuck. O(n).
```python
def can_jump(nums):
    reach = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if i > reach: return False
        reach = max(reach, i + x)
    return True
```

Minimum removals = total - maximum non-overlapping set. Greedy: sort by end, keep each interval that starts after the last kept end.
```python
def erase_overlaps(iv):
    iv.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]); end, keep = float("-inf"), 0
    for s, e in iv:
        if s >= end: keep += 1; end = e
    return len(iv) - keep
```
